why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
claim: The rotary's speed switch decides which of the type's two high-rotor rate bytes the rotor follows, and it turns over between 63 and 64 rather than at the 0x7F the page prints against it. Below that it is the slow byte, at every one of the 8 settings asked there; at and above it the fast byte, at every one of the 5, and the two arms are 0.84 Hz and 9.94 Hz apart so nothing turns on a small difference. With the switch on the fast arm the fast byte moves the rotor over the same printed table the slow byte was closed on -- ten settings, none of them further from an entry than the arrival gap already measured -- and the slow byte stops moving it at all, sitting inside 0.0002 Hz across three settings that span the whole of its range. What the byte does not decide is the arrival: below where the rotor already was, the fast byte lands on its entry to two thousandths of a hertz, and above it the rotor stops short by the same six hundredths the slow byte stops short by. That is the sign the mechanism beside this one predicts -- a lag written as an arithmetic right shift underflows climbing and floors falling -- and nothing here was fitted to it. Both of the readings this left standing were asked and both fell. The turnover is the machine's rather than this type's: the other type that prints the parameter turns over between the same two settings, with the same two rates under it. And the arrival is not the byte's: the same setting of the same byte stops short when it is written a third of a second after the switch and lands on its entry when it is written two seconds after it, which places the rotor between 4.05 and 4.25 Hz at the shorter gap.
named: a two-state parameter decoded from the top bit of its byte, selecting which of two entries of one rate table a rotor is sent to
adds: Two rate bytes of this type had no reading at all, and the reason was not that the address was wrong. It is that a value the store accepted never reached the state, which nothing in a record can show and only a page can say. What this adds beyond the two bytes is the turnover itself, which is a fact about how this machine decodes a switch and not about a rotary.
refutedBy: A take at a setting below 64 that returns the fast byte's rate, or one at or above it that returns the slow byte's. Either would mean the turnover is not where this puts it, and each of the thirteen settings asked was a place that could have happened. Also by the fast byte returning something that is not the printed table: it was read at ten settings and no entry was fitted, so any of the ten could have refused.

eraPriors.claim: A two-state parameter carried in a seven-bit byte is read by testing its top bit, which is one instruction and no comparison.
eraPriors.why: The states the page prints are 0x00 and 0x7F, whose top bits differ, and a machine of this period reading a switch out of a MIDI data byte has a bit test and not a range check to hand.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: The turnover sat anywhere but between 0x3F and 0x40 -- at 0x01, which would be a test against zero, or at 0x7F, which would be a test against the printed state itself. Both were asked and neither is where it is.

alternatives.reading: The boundary between landing on the entry and stopping short is a property of the byte or of the table rather than of where the rotor was when the byte arrived.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: It was asked, and one byte at one setting returns two rates. Written 0.3645 s after the switch, all four settings across the boundary stop short by about six hundredths of a hertz; written two seconds after it, all four land on their entry, and at eight seconds they agree with the two second pass to two ten thousandths. A property of the byte or of the table cannot move with when the byte was written, and this one moves the whole way -- from every setting short to every setting landing -- on a change that touches nothing but the gap.

alternatives.reading: The turnover is a test of the top bit rather than a comparison against 64, or against the halfway point of the printed range.

separatedBy.observable: Nothing a seven-bit byte can carry.

predicts.the top bit: slow below 64 and fast at and above it

separatedBy.sensitivity_here: Not applicable. Over the values this byte has, the top bit being set and the value being at least 64 are the same condition, so the two readings agree at all 128.
separatedBy.why_not_separable: They differ in which instruction the part runs and in nothing that comes out of the sockets. The claim does not rest on the difference: what it states is where the turnover is, and both readings put it there.

alternatives.reading: The other three types that print this parameter decode it some other way, so the turnover is this type's and not the machine's.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: It was asked on one of them. `11 07` prints a rotary beside a phaser and its switch at a different address, and it turns over between 63 and 64 as well: four settings below return 0.8374 Hz and four at and above return 9.9429 to 9.9432. The other two types are not asked, so what this rules out is the reading that the turnover is one type's -- a second type deciding it the same way is not two types deciding it differently.

extra.key: and the other spelling of a two state parameter
extra.text: This unit prints 58 two-state parameters and spells them two ways: four as 00/7F, all four of them a rotary's speed switch, and 54 as 00/01. The second spelling does not behave like the first. One of them has a sweep in this archive -- the amp switch of 01 10 -- and a whole filter appears between its 0 and its 1: the profile's largest band goes from 3.98 dB to -19.24 and its steepest slope from 1.78 dB per octave to 14.89. So that one is reached at 1 and does not wait for the top bit. Which rule it does follow is not read here and would need its own sweep. What is established is that the spelling is not decoration, and a run that writes a two-state byte without reading which spelling it has can get a null with nothing in the record to say the state was never reached.
